title: GEO in Perth: how WA businesses win AI answers
description: Perth is one of the easiest markets in Australia to become the AI recommendation in, and one of the fastest closing. Why isolation cuts both ways for WA businesses.
body:
Perth has a reputation as the most isolated capital city in the world. In generative engine optimisation, that isolation is an advantage, and most businesses here have about eighteen months to use it before it disappears.

Why Perth is unusually winnable

Answer engines form a view of a market by reading everything the web says about it. In Sydney or Melbourne, a category like conveyancing or commercial cleaning has hundreds of businesses producing content, thousands of reviews, and a decade of directory listings feeding the models. Forming a confident recommendation there means sorting a crowded field.

Perth categories are thinner. Ask an assistant who to use for a specific trade or professional service in the metro area and you will often get a hedged answer, sometimes naming a national chain with no real local presence, sometimes naming a business whose only advantage is an old directory listing. That hedging is the opportunity. In a thin market, the first business to give engines something solid to work with tends to become the default answer, and defaults are sticky.

The WA specifics that matter

A few things about this market change how the work is done.

  • Distance is a real search intent. People do not just ask who is best, they ask who services their corridor: north of the river, the Hills, Rockingham and Mandurah, Joondalup up to Yanchep. Businesses that state their service area plainly get named for those questions. Businesses that say "servicing Perth" get skipped for the suburb specific ones.
  • Resources adjacent work has its own language. A huge share of WA commerce touches mining, energy and the services around them. Buyers use industry terms, not consumer ones, and they ask questions loaded with compliance detail. Content written for a general audience does not get quoted for those queries.
  • FIFO changes buying patterns. Storage, vehicle care, home maintenance and property management all see demand shaped by rosters. Questions arrive at odd hours from people making decisions quickly, which favours businesses whose pricing and availability are readable without a phone call.
  • The two hour time zone gap. Perth runs behind the east coast, and a lot of national coverage and industry press is written from Sydney. WA businesses are systematically under represented in the sources engines cite. Local publications, WA industry bodies and community forums matter more here than they would elsewhere.

What actually moves the needle here

The order of work in a Perth engagement is usually different from an east coast one. Local proof comes first because it is scarce and it is the fastest route to being named.

That means Google Business Profile completeness and consistency across every directory the models read, then reviews on the platform your category actually uses, then pages that answer the suburb and corridor questions directly. Only after that do we go after industry publications and broader authority. In a crowded market you need authority to break through. In a thin one, clarity beats authority for the first year.

In a thin market, the first business to give engines something solid to work with becomes the default. Defaults are hard to dislodge.

The window is closing

The national agencies have noticed. Categories in Perth that were wide open eighteen months ago now have one or two businesses producing genuinely good answer led content, and those businesses are already being named consistently. Once an engine has settled on a recommendation and that recommendation keeps getting picked, the pattern reinforces itself.

The businesses that move now are buying a position that gets more expensive every quarter they wait. If you want to know what the engines currently say about your category in Perth, that is exactly what our free audit shows you, and you keep the findings either way.

title: What is GEO? A plain English guide for owners
description: Generative engine optimisation explained without the jargon: what changed, why the answer replaced the results page, and what it means for how customers find you.
body:
Ask ten people what GEO stands for and you will get ten slightly different definitions, which tells you how new this discipline is. Here is ours: generative engine optimisation is the work of getting your company named when an AI assistant answers your customers' questions.

That is the whole thing. Everything else is technique.

What actually changed

For twenty years, finding a product or a service meant typing a few words into a search box and scanning a page of links. The links competed for your click, and an entire industry, SEO, grew up around winning that competition.

Then assistants arrived. When someone asks ChatGPT which project management tool suits a small construction firm, or asks Perplexity who makes the most durable hiking boots, they do not get ten links. They get a short, confident answer that names one, two, maybe three companies. Google itself now answers many searches the same way, with an AI Overview sitting above the results it used to send you to.

The competition did not disappear. It moved. It used to happen on the results page, in front of the customer. Now it happens inside the model, before the customer ever sees anything.

Why this is bigger than it looks

A results page is forgiving. Position four still gets traffic. A distinctive brand can win the click from below a bigger rival. An answer is not forgiving. If the assistant names two companies and you are the third, you were never in the conversation, and you will not appear in any analytics report as a lost visitor. You simply were not mentioned.

Ten blue links had room for everyone. An answer has room for one or two names.

The upside is just as sharp. Companies that are consistently named become the default. The assistant recommends them, the customer arrives already half convinced, and every conversation starts warmer.

What GEO work actually involves

In practice, the work breaks into four parts.

  • Knowing what the engines say. Asking them your buyers' questions, at scale and on a schedule, and recording who gets named.
  • Being readable and trustworthy. Structured data, clear entity signals and pages that answer questions directly instead of burying the answer under a thousand words of preamble.
  • Being cited elsewhere. Engines lean heavily on sources they already trust: review platforms, industry publications, directories and communities. If those sources do not mention you, the engine has little reason to.
  • Measuring what it produces. Share of answer, assistant referred traffic and the enquiries behind it.

Is this just SEO with a new name?

Partly, and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something. Good technical foundations, useful content and a real reputation help you in both worlds. But the emphasis shifts hard. Rankings stop being the goal. Evidence, consistency across the wider web, and being quotable matter far more, and some old SEO habits, like publishing large volumes of thin keyword pages, now actively work against you.

If you want to know where you stand today, that is exactly what our free audit shows you: the questions your buyers ask, the names the engines give, and the distance between them and you.

title: GEO in Sydney: winning answers in Australia's hardest market
description: Sydney categories are crowded, well documented and fiercely contested. Why generic content fails here, and what actually earns an AI recommendation.
body:
Sydney is the most contested market in the country for AI answers, and the reason is straightforward: engines have more information about Sydney businesses than about businesses anywhere else in Australia. More competitors, more reviews, more press, more forum threads. When a model has abundant evidence, it becomes selective rather than generous.

What abundance does to answers

In a thin market an engine will name whoever it can find. In Sydney it has ten plausible candidates for every question and has to choose. That choice runs on differentiation, not volume. The businesses that get named are the ones whose evidence points clearly at a specific thing, and the ones that get skipped are the ones whose evidence says they do everything for everyone.

This is the single most common failure we see in Sydney audits. A firm that is genuinely excellent across six service lines writes about all six equally, and the engine reads that as a generalist. Meanwhile a smaller competitor that talks about one of those six relentlessly gets the recommendation for it.

Geography is the sharpest filter

Sydney is not one market. Buyers ask about the inner west, the north shore, the eastern suburbs, the Hills, the Shire, Parramatta and the greater west, and they treat those as different worlds because in practice they are. Travel time here is a genuine purchase criterion.

Businesses that name their actual catchment get named back. Businesses that claim all of Sydney compete against everyone and win nothing. If you genuinely serve the whole basin, the answer is not to hide it, it is to build separate substantial pages for the areas that matter commercially rather than one thin page per suburb, which engines read as filler and increasingly ignore.

The competitive intensity cuts both ways

Everything is harder in Sydney: the citations cost more to earn, the review counts you need are higher, the content has to be better because your competitors are also producing good content. But there are two advantages that make the work worth doing.

  • The prizes are bigger. Category leadership in a Sydney vertical is worth several times what it is worth in a smaller capital, because the volume behind it is enormous.
  • The sources are richer. Sydney has more trade press, more active professional communities, more review activity and more journalists covering local industries. There are simply more places to earn a citation, and engines read all of them.

What we do differently here

Sydney engagements lead with differentiation rather than coverage. Before any content gets written we work out which questions you can realistically own, which means being honest about the ones you cannot. Then we build depth on the winnable ones until the engines associate you with them unambiguously.

In a crowded market, being the obvious answer to one question beats being a plausible answer to twenty.

Authority work matters more here than anywhere else in the country, because when several businesses all have good content, the tiebreaker is which one the trusted sources talk about. That is slow work, and it is why we take one client per market: two Sydney competitors cannot both be the answer, and pretending otherwise wastes everyone's money.

If you want to see where you currently sit in your Sydney category, the audit will show you exactly who the engines name today and what stands between you and that position.

title: How AI assistants decide who to recommend
description: Assistants don't rank pages, they weigh evidence. A look at the signals that decide which companies get named in an answer and which get left out.
body:
When an assistant answers a buying question, it is not running your website through a ranking formula. It is doing something closer to what a well read friend does: recalling everything it has absorbed about a market and summarising the consensus. Understanding that difference is the foundation of all useful GEO work.

Two moments that decide everything

Your company gets its chance to be the answer at two different moments.

The first is training. Models learn from enormous snapshots of the web, and what they absorb about your category hardens into a kind of long term memory. If the pages, reviews and discussions in that snapshot consistently associate your name with your specialty, the model carries that association everywhere.

The second is retrieval. Most assistants now search the live web before answering, skim a handful of sources they trust, and compose the answer from what those sources say. This is the moment you can influence in weeks rather than years, because it depends on a small set of pages the engine actually reads.

The signals that seem to matter

Nobody outside the labs knows the exact recipe, and anyone claiming certainty is guessing. But watching thousands of answers across categories, clear patterns repeat.

  • Consensus across independent sources. One glowing page about you is noise. The same claim appearing on your site, in reviews, in a trade publication and in a community thread is a fact the engine can repeat safely.
  • Specificity. Engines prefer recommending the specialist for the question asked. The company that is precisely described wins the precise question.
  • Quotable pages. A page that answers a question in its first two sentences gives the model something to lift. A page that teases the answer to hold your attention gives it nothing.
  • Recency where it counts. For questions where the answer changes, engines favour sources that look maintained: updated data, current pricing, this year's review.
  • A clean entity. Consistent name, description and details everywhere you appear. Confusion about who you are is the fastest way to be left out of an answer that needs confidence.

What gets companies excluded

Just as instructive is who the engines quietly drop. Companies whose web presence contradicts itself. Companies whose only evidence is their own marketing. Companies whose category is described one way on their site and a different way everywhere else. The model is composing an answer it must stand behind, and ambiguity reads as risk.

The engine is not asking who shouts loudest. It is asking who it can name without being wrong.

What to do with this

Almost everything practical in GEO falls out of the paragraph above. Make the claim you want repeated, make it specific, and then make it true in as many independent, trusted places as possible. That is slower than gaming a ranking used to be, and far more durable once it is done, because a consensus, once formed, is hard for a competitor to dislodge.

If you want to see which claims the engines currently repeat about your market, and whose name is attached to them, that is what our free audit maps.

title: How to audit your own brand in ChatGPT in 30 minutes
description: A step by step method for finding out what AI assistants currently say about your company, using nothing but the free versions and a spreadsheet.
body:
Most companies have never checked what AI assistants say about them. Not once. They will happily pay for rank tracking on searches nobody performs any more, while the answers actually shaping their buyers' shortlists go completely unexamined.

Here is how to check, properly, in about half an hour, with free tools.

Step one: write the questions your buyers ask

Not keywords. Questions, phrased the way a person would type them into an assistant. Get fifteen to twenty of them. The best sources are your own sales calls, your support inbox and the first email a new enquiry sends you.

Aim for a spread across three types:

  • Category questions. Who is the best provider of X in Y, what are the top options for Z.
  • Problem questions. How do I solve the thing your product solves, without naming your category at all.
  • Brand questions. What does your company do, is it any good, how does it compare to a named competitor.

Step two: ask them in a clean session

This matters. Assistants personalise based on your history, so asking from your usual logged in account gives you a flattering and useless result. Use a fresh session, a logged out window, or temporary chat mode. You want the answer a stranger gets.

Run the same questions through at least three engines. ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini will give you a genuine spread, and Perplexity has the advantage of showing its sources, which tells you where the others are probably drawing from too.

Step three: record it in a way you can compare

A spreadsheet with one row per question and one column per engine. In each cell record three things: whether you were named, who else was named, and which sources were cited if the engine shows them.

Do not summarise as you go. Paste the actual text. Patterns become obvious across twenty raw answers that are invisible in your impression of them.

Step four: read it for the three things that matter

Your share. Count the questions where you were named at all. That number, out of twenty, is your rough share of answer. Most companies scoring their own category for the first time land somewhere between one and four.

Who beats you. Tally which competitors appear most. Frequently the winner is not your biggest rival but a smaller company that publishes more clearly.

What the engines get wrong. This is the highest value output of the exercise. Wrong service lines, outdated locations, an old business name, a capability you dropped years ago, or a claim about your pricing that has never been true. Each error traces back to a source you can go and fix.

The errors are the gift. Every one is a specific, fixable reason an engine is hedging about you.

Step five: do it again next month

One run is an anecdote. The value is in the trend, and answers drift more than people expect. Same questions, same engines, same clean session, once a month, in the same spreadsheet.

If this sounds like something you would rather not maintain by hand, that is fair, and it is most of what our free audit does, at greater scale and across more engines. But do the thirty minute version first. It will tell you whether this is a problem worth paying anyone to solve.

title: GEO in Melbourne: a city of specialists
description: Melbourne buyers research deeply and reward specificity. Why the city's culture of specialisation makes it unusually rewarding for GEO done properly.
body:
Melbourne rewards specialists. It is a city where a business can build a serious reputation for doing one narrow thing exceptionally, and where customers actively look for that rather than defaulting to the biggest name. That cultural habit maps almost perfectly onto how answer engines choose who to recommend.

Why specificity wins here

Engines are looking for the clearest match to a question. A Melbourne buyer rarely asks who does design, they ask who does brand identity for hospitality, or packaging for small batch producers. Those questions have precise answers, and the businesses that have documented their speciality get handed them.

We see this pattern across Melbourne categories: hospitality suppliers, trades working on period homes, allied health, professional services in specific industries. The market has already sorted itself into niches. The businesses losing AI answers are usually the ones whose websites describe them more broadly than their actual practice, which confuses an engine trying to make a precise recommendation.

The inner and outer divide

Melbourne's geography splits buying behaviour more sharply than most cities. Inner north, inner east, bayside, the outer east, the west and the growth corridors all behave differently, and buyers say so in their questions. A business with genuine inner north depth should say that plainly rather than claiming the whole metro area, because the engine will match the specific claim to the specific question.

There is also a strong regional dimension. Geelong, Ballarat, Bendigo and the Mornington Peninsula are meaningful markets in their own right, and businesses that serve them from Melbourne routinely fail to say so in a way engines can read.

Melbourne's citation landscape

This is a well documented city. Melbourne has active industry communities, strong local publications, hospitality and design press, and a culture of writing things down. That gives you more places to earn the independent mentions engines lean on than almost anywhere in the country outside Sydney.

  • Industry and trade press. Most Melbourne sectors have at least one publication engines read regularly.
  • Awards and guides. Melbourne runs on them, and being listed in credible ones is exactly the sort of independent evidence a model looks for.
  • Community forums. Suburb level and interest level communities here are unusually active and unusually detailed.
Melbourne buyers were already asking for specialists. The engines just made that preference machine readable.

The practical takeaway

If you run a Melbourne business, the highest value thing you can do is narrow what you claim until it matches what you are genuinely best at, then build real depth there. It feels counterintuitive to say less, and it is the single change that most reliably moves a Melbourne business into the answer.

Our audit maps which niche questions in your category currently go to competitors and which are still unclaimed. It costs nothing, and in this market the unclaimed ones are usually more valuable than they look.

title: Share of answer: the number that replaces rankings
description: Position three on Google meant something. Being one of two names in an AI answer means more. How to measure the metric that actually tracks the new buying journey.
body:
Every discipline gets the metric it deserves. SEO got rankings: where do we sit for this keyword? The question made sense when a results page was the battlefield. It makes very little sense now, because the customer increasingly never sees a results page.

The number that matters now is simpler and harsher: when buyers ask the questions that lead to your product, how often are you in the answer? We call it share of answer, and it is the single figure we judge our own work by.

How to measure it honestly

The method is straightforward, and the discipline is in doing it properly.

  • Start from real questions, not keywords. Nobody asks an assistant "best accounting software UK". They ask what a small consultancy should use for invoicing, or whether a certain tool handles their country's tax rules. Collect the questions your actual buyers ask, from sales calls, support tickets and your own team.
  • Ask across engines. ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude and Google's AI Overviews answer differently and are used by different people. A share that only covers one engine is a partial truth.
  • Ask repeatedly. Answers vary between sessions and drift over weeks. A single spot check is an anecdote. A schedule of the same questions, asked the same way, is a measurement.
  • Record competitors, not just yourself. Share is relative. Knowing you appear in three answers out of ten matters less than knowing a rival appears in eight.

Reading the number

Share of answer behaves differently from rankings, and the differences are worth internalising. It moves slowly, then suddenly, because engines form consensus rather than reorder a list. It rewards depth in a niche over breadth across many. And it compounds: once you are the name an engine gives, users act on the recommendation, and that behaviour reinforces the pattern.

Rankings told you where you stood in a queue. Share of answer tells you whether you exist in the conversation.

Tie it to money or ignore it

A share of answer number floating on its own is as decorative as a ranking report ever was. It earns its keep when you connect it to the rest of the funnel: assistant referred sessions, the enquiries they produce, and what those enquiries close at. In our experience assistant referred enquiries convert unusually well, because the customer arrives pre sold by a recommendation they trust more than an advert.

That connected picture, share, traffic, enquiries, revenue, is what a GEO report should look like. If your current agency cannot show it to you, ask them why.

title: Why reviews now matter more than backlinks
description: Backlinks were the currency of search rankings. Answer engines weigh a different kind of evidence, and most companies are under invested in it.
body:
For two decades, the answer to "how do we rank" involved backlinks. They were the closest thing search had to a vote of confidence, and an entire industry grew around acquiring them.

Answer engines changed the weighting. Links still matter, because they still help a model find and trust a page. But when an assistant is deciding which company to name, review consensus does more work than link volume, and most companies have their investment the wrong way round.

Why the shift happened

A link is a signal that someone thought a page was worth pointing at. A review is a statement about whether a business is actually good, written by someone who used it. When a model is composing a recommendation it must stand behind, the second kind of evidence is more directly useful.

Reviews also have three properties engines love. They are numerous, so patterns are statistically meaningful. They are recent, so they say something about the business now. And they are specific, so they support precise claims: not just that a company is good, but that it is good at a particular thing, for a particular kind of customer.

What engines actually extract from reviews

Not just the star rating. Modern models read the text and pull out themes.

  • Recurring specifics. If forty reviews mention that you turn work around quickly, the engine can confidently recommend you for urgent jobs.
  • Who you suit. Reviews reveal customer type in a way marketing copy never does.
  • Consistency over time. A steady flow beats a burst, which reads as either a campaign or a manipulation.
  • How you handle problems. Thoughtful responses to negative reviews are strong evidence of reliability. A wall of perfect scores with no dissent reads as less credible than a strong average with a few honest complaints handled well.

The practical rebalance

If you are spending on link acquisition and doing nothing systematic about reviews, you are optimising for the previous era. A reasonable split for most businesses is to put the majority of the effort into a consistent review habit and the remainder into earning genuine mentions in sources your industry actually trusts.

By systematic, we mean a defined moment in your delivery process where the ask happens, every time, to every satisfied customer, on the one platform that matters in your category. Not a campaign. A habit.

A link says someone noticed you. A review says someone chose you and it worked out.

The line you do not cross

Never buy reviews, never incentivise them, and never write them. Beyond the legal exposure, which in Australia is real and enforced, engines are increasingly good at detecting the patterns that fake reviews produce: clustered timing, similar phrasing, reviewer accounts with no other history. Getting flagged does not just cost you the fake reviews, it devalues the genuine ones alongside them.

The slow, honest version compounds. The fast version eventually costs you the asset you were trying to build.

title: GEO in Brisbane: getting ahead of a growth market
description: Brisbane is growing fast and its categories are still forming. Why the next few years decide which businesses become the default AI recommendation.
body:
Brisbane is in an unusual position. It is big enough that its categories matter commercially, still loose enough that most of them have no established AI answer, and growing fast enough that whoever claims a position now will be defending it against a much larger market later.

A market still forming

Ask an assistant a Brisbane specific buying question today and the answers are noticeably less settled than the equivalent Sydney or Melbourne query. You get more hedging, more national chains named by default, and more variation between engines. That variation is the tell: the models have not formed a consensus, because the evidence is not there yet.

Consensus is what GEO builds. When the same business keeps appearing in reviews, local press, industry listings and community discussion, the engines converge on it. In Brisbane that convergence has not happened in most categories, which means the cost of becoming the answer is lower right now than it will ever be again.

What is specific about Brisbane

  • Population growth changes the questions. A lot of Brisbane search intent comes from people who are new to the city and have no existing relationships. They ask open questions, they have no default provider, and they take recommendations at face value. That is the ideal audience for an AI answer to influence.
  • Construction and infrastructure are reshaping demand. Everything connected to building, fitting out, moving and servicing new development is seeing structural demand growth, and the businesses in those categories are mostly not documented well enough for engines to distinguish between them.
  • The corridors matter. Brisbane buyers think in terms of north side, south side, the bay side, Ipswich and the corridors out to the coasts. Service area clarity is worth as much here as it is in Perth.
  • Climate drives predictable seasonal questions. Storm season, humidity, flooding and heat generate recurring, high intent questions every year. Businesses that answer them properly get named every season, not once.

The 2032 factor, handled honestly

Every Brisbane marketing pitch now mentions the Olympics. The realistic version is this: the games will bring a wave of infrastructure spending, international attention and new residents, and it will increase competition in most local categories rather than simply increasing demand. Businesses that are already the established answer when that attention arrives will benefit from it. Businesses that start building position in 2031 will be doing it against a much noisier field.

The cheapest time to become the answer in Brisbane is while the engines are still hedging.

Where to start

In a forming market, the order is: get your entity clean and consistent everywhere, get review depth on the platform your category uses, answer the corridor and seasonal questions directly, then build citations. That sequence gets a Brisbane business into answers faster than authority chasing does, because authority is the slow part and clarity is the scarce part.

Our free audit shows you which Brisbane questions in your category currently have no confident answer. Those are the ones worth moving on first.

title: GEO vs SEO: what carries over and what doesn't
description: Twenty years of SEO habits are not wasted, but some of them now work against you. Where the disciplines overlap, where they split, and what to stop doing.
body:
The most common question we get from owners who built real organic traffic over the years: is all that work now worthless? The honest answer is no, but it is no longer sufficient, and a few of the habits that built it will actively hold you back if you keep them.

What transfers directly

The foundations of good SEO are the foundations of GEO too, and if you have them, you start ahead.

  • A crawlable, fast, well structured site. Retrieval based engines have to read your pages before they can quote them. Everything technical that helped Google helps them.
  • Genuine authority. Real reviews, earned media and a consistent reputation were the slow, unglamorous part of SEO. They are the core of GEO.
  • Content that actually answers things. If your pages were written for readers rather than crawlers, they are already close to quotable.

Where the disciplines split

The differences are less about tactics and more about what you are optimising for.

The unit of competition changed. SEO competed for positions on a page the user could see. GEO competes for inclusion in an answer the user cannot see being formed. There is no position four. You are named or you are absent.

The surface area changed. SEO focused overwhelmingly on your own site. In GEO, what the rest of the web says about you often outweighs what you say about yourself, because engines treat independent sources as evidence and your site as testimony.

The click stopped being the point. A growing share of answers end without any click at all. The recommendation itself is the value, which is why measuring visits alone now undercounts what visibility earns you.

What to stop doing

A few inherited habits now cost more than they return.

  • Volume publishing. Fifty thin posts a month made sense when every page was a lottery ticket. To an engine weighing evidence, a large body of shallow content dilutes your entity rather than strengthening it.
  • Keyword contortions. Pages twisted around exact match phrases read badly to humans and models alike. Engines answer questions, so write to questions.
  • Chasing every topic. Breadth worked when each ranking was independent. Consensus does not form around a generalist. Pick the questions you deserve to win and go deep.
SEO optimised what your site said. GEO optimises what the web agrees about you.

The practical takeaway

Keep the foundations, keep the honest content, and redirect the effort that went into rankings toward evidence: original data, real reviews, presence in the sources your engines cite. Do not run the two disciplines as rivals. Run them as one programme with a new definition of winning.

title: Schema markup for GEO: what actually helps
description: Structured data is having a second life. A practical guide to the markup that genuinely improves how answer engines read your business, and the kind that does nothing.
body:
Structured data spent years as a rich snippets tactic: add the markup, get the stars in search results. Its value now is different and larger. Schema is how you state facts about your business in a form a machine cannot misread.

Why it matters more for answers than for rankings

When an assistant composes an answer it needs facts it can assert confidently. Prose is ambiguous. Schema is not. A page that says "we have been serving the region for over two decades" leaves a model guessing. A page carrying a foundingDate leaves nothing to interpret.

Every ambiguity you remove is one fewer reason for an engine to hedge or pick a competitor whose details are clearer.

The markup worth implementing

  • Organization. The foundation. Legal name, alternate names, logo, founding date, contact points, and critically the sameAs links to your profiles elsewhere. This is how you tell an engine that the company on your site and the company in a directory are the same entity.
  • LocalBusiness. For anyone with a service area or premises. Address, hours, service area, price range. Get this exactly consistent with every other listing you have.
  • Service or Product. One per genuine offering, with clear descriptions and pricing where you can publish it.
  • FAQPage. Underrated for GEO. It hands an engine question and answer pairs in the exact shape it wants. Use it only for questions people genuinely ask.
  • Article with author. On every piece of content. Attribution is an evidence signal, and anonymous content is weaker evidence.
  • Review and AggregateRating. Only where you have genuine reviews to describe, and only where the platform's terms permit it.

What does not help

Marking up things that are not there. Inventing an aggregate rating, adding FAQ markup to questions nobody asks, or describing services you do not offer. Engines cross reference structured data against the visible page and against other sources. Markup that contradicts reality damages trust in everything else you have marked up.

Volume for its own sake does not help either. Six accurate types implemented properly beat twenty half filled ones.

The sameAs property deserves its own paragraph

If you implement one thing from this article, make it this. The sameAs array in your Organization schema lists every other place your business exists: your Google Business Profile, LinkedIn, industry directories, review platforms, Wikipedia or Wikidata if you are there.

This is the connective tissue of entity recognition. Without it an engine sees several possibly related listings. With it, it sees one business with corroborating evidence in many places, which is precisely the confidence it needs to name you.

Schema does not make your business better. It makes your business unmistakable, which is what a model needs before it will recommend you.

Getting it done

Validate everything with Google's Rich Results Test and Schema.org's validator before you ship. Then check it again after any site change, because template updates silently break markup more often than anyone expects. It is an afternoon of work for a developer and it is the highest certainty item on any GEO plan.

title: GEO for local service businesses
description: Trades, home services and local operators have a structural advantage in AI answers. Most are throwing it away with thin suburb pages.
body:
Local service businesses should be winning AI answers. The questions are simple, the buying decision is fast, the customer usually has no existing provider, and the field in any given suburb is small. Instead most are invisible, and the reason is almost always the same handful of mistakes.

The urgency advantage

A large share of local service demand is urgent: a blocked drain, a broken air conditioner in February, a locked door at midnight. Urgent buyers do the least research and accept the first credible recommendation. There is no channel where being the named answer converts better.

Urgent questions also have unusually clear shapes. Someone asking for an emergency plumber in a named suburb at 11pm is asking a question with a right answer, and an engine will give one if it can find a business that has stated availability, service area and response time plainly.

The suburb page mistake

Nearly every local business has been sold the same tactic: generate a page for every suburb, swap the name, publish two hundred of them. It worked adequately in old search. It actively hurts you now.

Engines treat near duplicate pages as low quality, and a site made mostly of them looks like filler. Worse, the pages say nothing an engine can use, because a suburb name inserted into boilerplate contains no information about whether you actually serve that suburb well.

The replacement is fewer, substantially different pages for the areas that genuinely matter to your business, each containing real specifics: response times to that area, jobs you commonly do there, the quirks of the local housing stock, any surcharge or travel consideration. Ten real pages outperform two hundred generated ones.

What to publish instead

  • Straight answers to your five most common phone questions. Whatever people ask before booking, answered in plain text, including the awkward ones about price.
  • Price guidance. Ranges, call out fees, what changes the number. Most competitors refuse to publish this, which makes the business that does the one an engine can answer with.
  • Availability and response reality. What after hours actually means, how fast you get to each area, what the wait is in peak season.
  • The problem content. How to tell whether a thing needs repair or replacement, what a noise means, what to do before the technician arrives. These get quoted constantly and they demonstrate competence.
Two hundred suburb pages tell an engine nothing. One honest pricing page tells it everything.

Reviews are the whole ballgame

In local services, review consensus outweighs everything else. A business with two hundred recent, detailed reviews will be recommended over a business with better content and twelve reviews, nearly every time. If you do nothing else, build a reliable habit of asking every satisfied customer, on the platform your category actually uses.

Our audit shows what assistants currently answer for the urgent questions in your area. For most local businesses, the recommendation currently goes to a competitor who simply published their prices.

title: Why original data is the fastest way into AI answers
description: Engines cite sources that know something the rest of the web doesn't. How one piece of genuine research can outwork a hundred blog posts, and how to produce it.
body:
Here is a pattern we see constantly in answer tracking: a mid sized company publishes one genuinely original piece of research, and within months it is being cited by engines in answers its far larger competitors used to own. Not because the company is famous. Because it produced the only real number in the room.

Why engines love data

An assistant composing an answer is hunting for things it can state with confidence. Opinions are everywhere and contradict each other. A specific figure from a named source is different: it is concrete, attributable and useful. When the only available answer to "what does X typically cost" or "how long does Y actually take" comes from your survey of your own market, the engine has one place to go, and it goes there repeatedly.

Better still, other publications cite data too. One good study earns mentions in trade press and newsletters, and each mention is another independent source associating your name with your subject. The engine sees consensus forming, and consensus is what gets you named.

You have more data than you think

Owners hear "original research" and imagine commissioning a polling firm. Usually the material is already sitting in the business.

  • Operational numbers. Real timelines, real cost ranges, real failure rates across hundreds of jobs. Anonymised and aggregated, this is the exact information buyers ask assistants for and almost nobody publishes.
  • A simple survey of your customers or industry. Fifty thoughtful responses to well designed questions beat a thousand responses to lazy ones.
  • Benchmarks from your own tools. If your product or process generates measurements, an annual report built on them can become the reference for your category.

Publishing it so it gets cited

The packaging decides whether the work pays. A few rules we follow on every study.

  • Lead with the finding. The headline number in the first paragraph, stated plainly, so it can be quoted without excavation.
  • Show the method. Sample size, time period, how it was gathered. Engines and journalists both check whether a number looks defensible.
  • Keep a stable home. One permanent page per study, updated annually, rather than a scatter of posts. Citations accumulate to an address.
  • Give it away. No gate, no email wall. A gated study cannot be read by the things you want quoting it.
In a war of opinions, the only measurement wins.

One caution: the data must be real, and the method must survive scrutiny. An invented statistic that gets cited widely is a reputational bomb with your name printed on it. The whole point is to be the source engines can trust. Earn it once and it keeps paying for years.

title: GEO in Adelaide: small market, large advantage
description: Adelaide's size is usually framed as a limitation. For generative engine optimisation it is close to ideal, and the maths explains why.
body:
Adelaide businesses are used to being told their market is small. In generative engine optimisation, small is the wrong frame. What matters is the ratio between how much demand a category has and how much evidence exists for the engines to sort it. On that measure Adelaide is one of the best value markets in Australia.

The maths of a winnable market

Becoming the answer requires a certain absolute quantity of evidence: enough reviews, enough content depth, enough independent mentions that a model can name you with confidence. That quantity does not scale down with city size. It is roughly the same job in Adelaide as in Sydney.

What does scale down is how much your competitors have already built. In a Sydney category you might need to outproduce twenty well resourced businesses. In the Adelaide equivalent you might need to outproduce three, and often none of them are actively trying. The work costs the same and buys far more.

Adelaide's specific strengths

  • Genuine industry clusters. Wine, defence, food production, health and higher education are real concentrations with their own publications, associations and buyer language. Clusters generate the sort of independent, specific coverage that engines treat as strong evidence.
  • Tight professional networks. Word travels in Adelaide, which means reputation is more consistent across sources. Engines like consistency, because contradictory evidence is what makes them hedge.
  • Manageable geography. Most Adelaide businesses can credibly service the whole metro area, which removes the service area fragmentation that complicates the work in Sydney and Perth.

The trap to avoid

The most common Adelaide mistake is assuming the local market is too small to bother documenting properly, and pointing all the marketing effort at interstate or national positioning instead. This backfires twice. You fail to claim the local answers that were sitting there for the taking, and you compete nationally without the evidence base to win.

Own your local category first. It is achievable, it produces revenue quickly, and the citations and reviews you build doing it are the same assets that make a national push viable later.

The evidence needed to become the answer barely changes with city size. The competition for it changes enormously.

What the first year looks like

An Adelaide engagement usually reaches category leadership faster than an east coast one, often inside nine months rather than eighteen. The work is the same: entity clarity, review depth, question led content, then citations in the local and industry sources engines read. There is simply less to overcome.

If you want to see how contested your Adelaide category actually is, the audit will show you who the engines name today. In our experience the answer surprises people, usually because it is nobody in particular.

title: Entity clarity: making engines certain who you are
description: Before an engine can recommend you it has to be sure you exist, what you do and that the mentions of you elsewhere are the same company. Most businesses fail this quietly.
body:
There is a step before optimisation that almost nobody audits: does the engine actually know who you are? Not whether it rates you highly. Whether it has a confident, single, correct picture of your business at all.

In our audits this is the most common blocker, and it is invisible from the inside because you know who you are.

What an entity is

An entity is the model's internal idea of your company: name, what you do, where, who runs it, what it is known for, and every source that mentions it. Recommendations are made about entities. If your entity is fuzzy, split across variants or contradicted by stale sources, an engine will hedge and name someone whose picture is clearer.

The four ways entities break

  • Name variants. Trading name, legal name, an abbreviation, an old name from before a rebrand, and the version with Pty Ltd. Each appearing in different places, none of them linked. The engine may be treating these as several companies, each with a fraction of your evidence.
  • Category drift. Your site says one thing, your directory listings say something broader, an old press mention says something else entirely. The model cannot decide what you actually do, so it does not recommend you for anything specific.
  • Location contradictions. An old address in a directory, a service area that expanded without the listings being updated, a closed branch that still shows as open somewhere.
  • Confusion with someone else. A similarly named business, often in another city or industry, whose information gets blended into yours. This one is more common than people expect and it is corrosive.

How to fix it

The work is unglamorous and it is the highest return item in most first months.

Pick one canonical form of everything. One name, one one sentence description, one address format, one phone number, one category. Write it down as a reference document.

Push it everywhere. Your site, your schema, your Google Business Profile, every directory, every social profile, every industry listing. Anywhere your business appears, it should appear identically.

Link the profiles together. The sameAs array in your Organization schema should list every one of them. This is what tells an engine these scattered listings describe one company.

Hunt down the stale records. Old addresses, dead branches, previous names, defunct directory entries. Correct them at the source or get them removed. This is tedious and it is often what unlocks everything else.

An engine will not confidently recommend a company it is not confident exists in one piece.

How to tell if this is your problem

Ask three assistants to describe your company and compare the answers. If they disagree with each other, contradict your website, mention things you stopped doing, or blend you with another business, your entity is the bottleneck. No amount of content will fix that, and fixing it often produces movement within weeks.

title: A practical GEO checklist you can run this month
description: Ten things any company can do in the next thirty days to show up better in AI answers, ordered by effort against impact, with no tools to buy.
body:
Most GEO advice is either theory or a sales pitch. This is neither: ten concrete actions, ordered roughly by effort against impact, that any company can start this month without buying a single tool. Do the first five and you will be ahead of most of your market.

1. Ask the engines about yourself

Spend an hour asking ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini the questions your buyers actually ask, and write down every answer. Who gets named? What does the engine believe about you, and is any of it wrong? This single exercise reframes the whole subject, because you stop guessing and start looking at the actual battlefield.

2. Fix what they get wrong

Wrong descriptions usually trace to stale or contradictory information: an old address, an outdated service list, a directory profile from a previous era of the business. Hunt down the sources of the error and correct them at the origin.

3. Make one page answer one question, immediately

Take your most valuable buying question and make sure a page on your site answers it in the first two sentences, in plain language, with specifics. Not a teaser, not a form gate. The direct answer, then the depth below it for humans who keep reading.

4. Standardise your entity everywhere

Same company name, same one sentence description, same core details, everywhere you appear: your site, social profiles, directories, review platforms. Every inconsistency is a small tax on the engine's confidence in naming you.

5. Add structured data to the pages that matter

Organisation, product, service and FAQ markup, correctly implemented on your key pages. It is unglamorous plumbing, it takes a developer an afternoon, and it makes you machine readable in exactly the way retrieval systems appreciate.

6. Get ten real reviews on the platform your market trusts

Engines cite review consensus constantly. Identify the one platform that matters in your category and ask your genuinely happy customers to write honest reviews there. Never buy reviews. Bought reviews are both an offence against the platforms and exactly the kind of pattern engines learn to discount.

7. Answer real questions in your community

Find where your buyers actually discuss the problem, often a subreddit, a forum, an industry Slack, and contribute genuinely useful answers under your real identity. Engines read these spaces. So do your customers.

8. Publish one number nobody else has

From your own operations: a real cost range, a real timeline, a real benchmark. Put it on a permanent page with your method. Original data is the single fastest way to become citable, and most of your competitors will never bother.

9. Refresh the dates that deserve it

Engines favour maintained sources for questions where answers change. Update your key pages with current facts and current dates, but only where something genuinely changed. Fake freshness is another pattern the engines are getting better at ignoring.

10. Set up a monthly measurement habit

The same questions, the same engines, once a month, recorded in a spreadsheet. Share of answer is a trend, not a snapshot, and the companies that win it are the ones that watch it.

None of this is magic. It is consistency, applied where the engines are actually looking.

If you would rather see the whole picture done properly in one pass, that is what our free audit is for. Either way, start this month. Consensus takes time to form, and it is forming right now, with or without you.

title: GEO on the Gold Coast: tourism, trades and transience
description: A market where most customers are new, most decisions are fast, and almost nobody has an existing provider. Why that makes AI answers unusually powerful.
body:
The Gold Coast has a customer base that keeps refreshing itself. Tourists, new residents, investors, seasonal workers and people relocating from down south all arrive without a plumber, a lawyer, a gym or a removalist. They have no existing relationship to fall back on, so they ask.

That makes this one of the highest leverage markets in the country for generative engine optimisation, because the recommendation an assistant gives is frequently the only input a buyer has.

Three overlapping markets

Businesses here usually serve some mix of three audiences, and they ask very different questions.

  • Visitors. Short horizon, high urgency, no local knowledge, heavily reliant on whatever the first answer says. They ask for the best, the closest and the open now.
  • New residents. Longer horizon, higher value, and actively building a full set of providers at once. Winning one of these is often worth years of revenue across multiple services.
  • Established locals and businesses. Smaller in number, but the ones who generate the reviews and word of mouth that make the other two groups' answers point at you.

Content that tries to speak to all three at once speaks clearly to none. The businesses winning here write separately for the visitor question and the resident question, because those are genuinely different searches.

Reviews carry more weight here than almost anywhere

When a buyer has no local knowledge and no network to ask, review consensus becomes the dominant signal, and engines know it. Gold Coast categories with heavy tourist demand are decided on review depth and recency more than on content quality.

The practical implication is that a systematic review habit is not a nice extra here, it is the core of the work. Recent, specific, plentiful reviews on the platform your category uses will do more for your share of answer than another twenty pages of content.

Seasonality is a content opportunity

Schoolies, winter arrivals from the southern states, storm season, the events calendar and holiday peaks all generate predictable spikes in specific questions. Most businesses react to these. The ones that get named have already published the answer and let it accumulate authority across seasons.

When a customer has no local network to ask, the assistant's answer is not one input among many. It is the whole decision.

The transience trap

The flip side of a refreshing customer base is that Gold Coast businesses churn too, and engines notice inconsistency. Closed locations, changed trading names, abandoned profiles and stale listings are unusually common here, and they make models hedge. A significant part of the early work in this market is simply cleaning up the contradictory record of a business that has moved, rebranded or expanded over the years.

Our audit will show you what the engines currently believe about your business, including anything they have wrong. That part alone is worth the call.

title: GEO for ecommerce: getting your products into answers
description: Shoppers are asking assistants what to buy instead of browsing category pages. What that changes about product content, reviews and comparison.
body:
Ecommerce spent fifteen years optimising for a shopper who browses. That shopper is being replaced by one who asks: what is the best option for my situation, and why. The answer they get names two or three products, and the rest of the market is not in the conversation.

What changes about product content

Product pages were written to persuade someone already looking at them. Now they need to inform a model deciding whether to mention you at all, which rewards different writing.

  • Specifications belong in text. Dimensions, materials, compatibility, capacity, care requirements. If it is only in an image or a spec sheet graphic, it does not exist to an engine.
  • Say who it is not for. Counterintuitive and highly effective. Stating the limits of a product lets a model recommend it confidently for the right situation, and confidence is what gets you named.
  • Answer the comparison question. Buyers ask how your product compares to alternatives. If you never address it, the engine uses a competitor's or a review site's framing instead of yours.
  • Use case over feature list. People ask by situation, not by specification. Content organised around situations matches more questions.

Reviews do double duty

Product reviews are simultaneously your conversion tool and your primary GEO evidence. Engines read them heavily for exactly the details product copy avoids: how it holds up over time, what surprised people, who it did not suit.

Which means review volume alone is not the goal. Reviews that mention specific use cases are worth more than generic praise, and prompting for specifics in your post purchase request measurably changes what engines can extract.

Category pages become guides

A traditional category page is a grid with a paragraph of text underneath. To an engine it is nearly content free. The version that earns citations is a genuine buying guide: what the options are, how to choose between them, what matters at different budgets, what the common mistakes are.

This feels like a lot of work for a page that used to be a filter interface. It is also the page most likely to be quoted when someone asks how to choose in your category.

The marketplace tension

If you sell through marketplaces as well as your own site, engines frequently cite the marketplace listing rather than you, because it carries more reviews and more traffic. You cannot fully prevent this, but you can make your own pages the better source by putting information there that the marketplace listing cannot hold: depth, comparison, guides, genuine expertise.

The shopper who browses is being replaced by one who asks. Category pages built for browsing have nothing to say to them.

Structured data is not optional here

Product schema with accurate price, availability and rating is the baseline. It is how an engine states a fact about your product without hedging, and in ecommerce the hedge usually costs you the mention.

Our audit shows which products in your category currently get named and where those recommendations are sourced from. It is frequently a review site rather than any retailer, which tells you exactly where the work needs to go.

title: The prompts your customers actually use
description: Keyword research does not survive the shift to assistants. How to find the real questions buyers ask, and why they look nothing like your keyword list.
body:
Keyword lists were built around how people type into a search box: short, clipped, stripped of context. Best accountant Perth. Commercial cleaning Sydney cost. Two to four words, no sentence.

Nobody talks to an assistant that way. They write sentences, they include their situation, and they ask for judgement. Optimising for the old phrasing means optimising for a question that is being asked less every month.

What a real prompt looks like

A search query might be "conveyancer Perth". The equivalent prompt is closer to: "We're buying our first place in the northern suburbs and settling in about six weeks. What should we look for in a conveyancer and roughly what should it cost?"

Notice what is in there that the keyword lacks. A situation, a constraint, a timeframe, two distinct questions and an implicit request for advice rather than a list. Content written for the keyword answers none of it. Content written for the prompt answers all of it and gets quoted.

Where to find the real ones

You cannot get these from a keyword tool, because the tools report search volume for search phrasing. You get them from the places people actually explain their situations.

  • Your sales calls. The first three minutes of a discovery call is a prompt, spoken aloud. Start writing them down verbatim.
  • Your inbox. First contact emails are close to perfect prompts, complete with context and constraints.
  • Your support tickets. Post purchase questions reveal what buyers did not understand beforehand, which is exactly what the next buyer will ask an assistant.
  • Community threads. Reddit, industry forums and local groups are full of people describing their situation and asking for recommendations. This is the closest public analogue to prompt behaviour, and engines read these threads too.
  • The assistants themselves. Ask one what people typically want to know before buying in your category. The answer is a serviceable starting list.

Turning prompts into content

Once you have thirty real prompts, group them by underlying need rather than by wording. Several differently phrased prompts usually share one answer, and one substantial page answering that need properly will match all of them. This is the opposite of the old approach of one page per keyword variant.

Then write the answer the way you would say it: lead with the direct response, follow with the reasoning, include the numbers, name the trade offs honestly.

Your customers stopped typing fragments. Content written for fragments has stopped matching them.

The awkward questions matter most

The prompts businesses least want to answer publicly, about price, about who they are not right for, about how they compare to a cheaper option, are the ones assistants most need an answer to. Whoever answers them becomes the source. Usually nobody does, which makes it the cheapest position on the board.

title: GEO in Canberra: procurement, professionals and precision
description: A market dominated by government adjacent buyers who research carefully and buy on credentials. Why precision beats persuasion in the ACT.
body:
Canberra buys differently from every other Australian city. A large share of commercial activity runs directly or indirectly through government, which means buyers are frequently professionals following a process rather than owners following instinct. They research before they engage, they check credentials, and they document what they find.

For generative engine optimisation, that changes what evidence matters.

Credentials are the evidence

In most markets, review consensus is the strongest independent signal. In Canberra, formal credentials often outrank it: panel arrangements, security clearances, certifications, professional registrations, association memberships and demonstrable experience with comparable organisations.

Engines can only use these if they are stated plainly and corroborated elsewhere. A capability buried in a downloadable PDF is invisible. The same capability stated clearly on a page, listed in an association directory and mentioned in an industry publication becomes something a model will repeat.

The questions are unusually specific

Canberra buying questions carry more qualification than consumer ones. They name the sector, the compliance requirement, the scale and the constraint in a single sentence. Content written at a general level does not match them.

  • Pages should answer the qualified question, not the broad category one
  • Compliance and clearance requirements belong in readable text, not in attachments
  • Comparable past work matters more than volume of past work
  • Professional association listings are high value citations in this market specifically

The private market is underserved

Because so much attention goes to government work, the ordinary Canberra consumer market is one of the thinnest in the country in terms of documented evidence. Trades, health, hospitality, home services and professional services for individuals are frequently answered by engines with hedged responses or by national brands with no local presence.

For a business serving Canberra residents rather than agencies, that is an open field. The population is affluent, stable and highly connected, and almost nobody in these categories is producing the sort of content engines can quote.

In a market of professional buyers, the recommendation is only useful if the reasons behind it survive scrutiny.

Precision over persuasion

The tone that works here is factual. Canberra buyers, and the engines serving them, respond to specific claims with visible support: what you do, who you have done it for, what qualifies you, what it costs. Marketing language that would pass in another market reads as evasive to a professional buyer and gives a model nothing citable.

Our audit shows what the engines currently say when someone asks a qualified question in your category. In Canberra the gap between what a business can actually do and what the engines know about it is usually the widest we see anywhere.

title: GEO for professional services firms
description: Accountants, consultants, agencies and advisory firms sell judgement. Making judgement legible to an answer engine is a specific discipline.
body:
Professional services firms have a harder GEO problem than product businesses, and it is not the one they usually think it is. The difficulty is not competition. It is that what they sell, judgement applied to a specific situation, resists being written down in a form an engine can quote.

The generality trap

Ask most firms what they do and you get something like "we provide tailored solutions to help our clients achieve their objectives". Every word of that is defensible and none of it is usable. An engine cannot recommend a firm for anything specific on the strength of it.

The firms winning answers have done something uncomfortable: they have stated plainly what they are for and, by implication, what they are not for. A firm known for one sector at one scale gets recommended precisely. A firm that could serve anyone gets recommended to no one.

Publish the thinking, not the credentials

Professional sites are heavy on qualifications and light on point of view. But credentials are table stakes and every competitor has them. What differentiates you, and what an engine can quote, is your actual position on the questions clients face.

  • What you think most firms get wrong about a common problem
  • How you would approach a decision your clients regularly face
  • What the real trade offs are between two options everyone talks about
  • What something typically costs and what makes it cost more

This is genuine intellectual property given away, and that is the point. The firm that publishes the clearest thinking on a question becomes the source engines cite when the question is asked.

Fees are the hardest and most valuable page

Almost no professional firm publishes fee information, for defensible reasons: every engagement differs and a number without context invites the wrong comparison. But buyers ask about cost constantly and assistants need something to say.

The workable version is ranges with the variables explained: what a typical engagement of a given type costs, what moves it up, what moves it down, what a minimum looks like. This qualifies your enquiries as much as it wins them, which most firms discover they wanted anyway.

Buyers ask about fees whether you publish them or not. The only question is whether the answer comes from you.

Named people beat the firm

Engines handle individual expertise well. A partner with a consistent public presence, articles under their own byline, speaking appearances and a properly linked professional profile becomes an entity in their own right, and the firm inherits the credibility.

Anonymous corporate content is weaker evidence than the same content with a real author attached. Attribute everything.

Where to start

Pick the one thing you are genuinely best known for. Write the definitive piece on it, under a named author, with real numbers and a clear position. Then get that person mentioned in the industry sources your peers read. That sequence, repeated a few times, is how a professional firm becomes an answer.

title: GEO in Hobart and Tasmania: the thinnest data in the country
description: Tasmanian categories have so little documentation that engines routinely get them wrong. That is a problem and an opportunity in equal measure.
body:
Ask an AI assistant a Tasmanian buying question and you will frequently get an answer that is out of date, mainland focused, or quietly wrong. Businesses that closed years ago still get recommended. Mainland companies with no Tasmanian presence get named for local services. The reason is simple: there is not enough current information for the model to do better.

Why the data is so thin

Tasmania has a small population spread across a large area, fewer local publications than it once had, and a business culture that runs heavily on word of mouth. Word of mouth is excellent for business and invisible to an engine. A firm can be the obvious choice in Hobart, known to everyone in its industry, and be entirely absent from the evidence a model reads.

This produces the strange situation where the actual market leader in a Tasmanian category is often not the AI recommended one, because the recommendation is built on whatever fragments happen to exist online.

What this means practically

  • Correcting the record comes first. Before building anything new, the priority is fixing what engines currently believe: stale listings, closed competitors, wrong service areas, outdated details.
  • The bar to become the answer is genuinely low. A well structured site, a consistent entity, a real review base and a handful of local citations can be enough to become the default in a Tasmanian category. That combination would be a starting point in Melbourne.
  • North and south are separate markets. Hobart and Launceston behave differently and buyers ask about them separately. The north west coast is different again. Businesses serving the whole state should say which parts properly.
  • Tourism questions are disproportionately valuable. Visitors arrive with no local knowledge at all, so the answer they get carries enormous weight, and the volume is far larger than the resident population suggests.

The industries where this bites hardest

Tourism and hospitality, food and beverage production, aquaculture, forestry services, trades and construction, and the professional services around them all share the same pattern: strong real world reputations, weak documented evidence. Producers with genuine national profile in their category are frequently unknown to engines answering questions about that category.

In Tasmania the market leader and the AI recommendation are often two different businesses. That gap is the whole opportunity.

Small market, fast results

Tasmanian engagements tend to show movement faster than anywhere else we work, because there is so little to displace. The trade off is that the sources are fewer, so the citation work requires more creativity: state industry bodies, local press, tourism operators, regional publications and genuine community presence rather than a long list of trade titles.

If you run a Tasmanian business, it is worth simply asking an assistant about your category and reading what comes back. Our audit does that systematically, and the findings are yours whether you work with us or not.

title: Nine GEO mistakes we see in almost every audit
description: The recurring errors keeping companies out of AI answers, roughly in the order of how much they cost and how easily they are fixed.
body:
We have run this audit enough times to know what we are going to find before we start. The same mistakes recur across industries, countries and company sizes. Here they are, roughly ordered by how much they cost against how easily they are fixed.

1. Never having looked

The most common one. Companies with sophisticated marketing operations who have never once asked an assistant what it says about them. You cannot manage what you have not measured, and this measurement takes thirty minutes.

2. A split or contradictory entity

Name variants, old addresses, stale directory records and profiles that disagree with each other. The engine is not sure you are one company, so it hedges. This is unglamorous to fix and frequently produces the fastest movement.

3. Claiming too much

Firms that list every service they can technically perform, hoping to match more queries. The effect is the opposite: the engine reads a generalist and recommends the specialist instead. Narrowing what you claim usually widens what you get named for.

4. Answers buried below the fold of the argument

Content that builds to its answer over eight hundred words of preamble, in the old style designed to hold attention. Engines quote the direct statement. Put it in the first two sentences and use the rest for the reasoning.

5. Facts locked inside PDFs and images

Capability statements, price lists, spec sheets and service tables that exist only as downloads or graphics. Everything a buyer needs, in a format engines cannot read. Moving this content into plain page text is often an afternoon's work with disproportionate effect.

6. No structured data, or worse, wrong structured data

Missing Organization markup, absent sameAs links, or markup describing things that are not on the page. The first is a missed opportunity. The third actively damages trust.

7. Treating reviews as a passive outcome

Waiting for reviews to happen rather than building a habit of asking. Review consensus is among the strongest signals an engine uses, and most companies leave it entirely to chance.

8. Volume publishing

Large quantities of thin content produced on a schedule, often now generated. It dilutes your entity, it gives models nothing worth quoting, and engines are visibly getting better at discounting it. One substantial piece with original data outperforms thirty filler posts, and costs less to produce.

9. Refusing to publish prices

The most consistently costly omission we see. Buyers ask about cost in nearly every category. Companies that publish honest ranges with the variables explained become the source engines answer with. Companies that do not get replaced by a competitor who did.

None of these are sophisticated problems. That is exactly why so few companies have fixed them.

The pattern behind the pattern

Almost every item on this list is a version of the same thing: being vague where you could be specific. Engines reward specificity because specificity is what lets them answer confidently. Most marketing instinct pushes the other way, toward keeping options open and claims broad.

If you only take one thing from this list, take that. Then go and ask an assistant about your company and see which of the nine you recognise.

title: GEO in Darwin and the Northern Territory
description: A remote market with high stakes purchases, a transient population and almost no competition for AI answers. What that combination means.
body:
The Northern Territory is the most extreme version of a pattern we see across regional Australia: real commercial demand, genuinely high value transactions, and almost no documented evidence for engines to work from. Most NT categories have no established AI answer at all.

Who is actually asking

NT search intent skews toward people without local knowledge, which is exactly the audience an AI recommendation influences most.

  • New arrivals. Defence postings, health and education placements, mining and construction contracts and government transfers bring a constant flow of people who need a full set of providers immediately and know nobody.
  • Businesses operating remotely. Companies servicing remote communities, stations and sites need suppliers who genuinely understand the logistics, and they research carefully because getting it wrong is expensive.
  • Visitors. Tourism is highly seasonal and almost entirely made up of people with no local network.

Logistics is the buying criterion

In most markets, questions are about quality and price. In the Territory a large share are about whether you can actually get there, how long it takes, and what it costs to service somewhere remote. Businesses that answer those questions plainly get named for them, and most competitors never address them in writing at all.

Stating your real service radius, your remote capability, your lead times and how you handle the wet season is not administrative detail here. It is the substance of the buying decision, and it is exactly the sort of specific, factual content an engine can quote with confidence.

Seasonality is structural

The wet and dry seasons reshape demand across nearly every NT category, and the questions change with them. Access, timing, weather contingency and availability all become live concerns for half the year. A business that has published clear seasonal guidance becomes the answer during the period when those questions spike, every year.

In a market where almost nobody has documented anything, being specific about logistics is a competitive advantage.

The scarcity problem, honestly stated

The hard part of NT work is citations. There are fewer publications, fewer industry bodies and fewer review platforms with meaningful local depth. The usual playbook of earning mentions across many sources does not have as many sources to work with.

What compensates is that the competition is not doing it either. A modest citation base, combined with genuinely clear content and a consistent entity, is frequently enough to become the default answer in an NT category. That is a proposition that no longer exists in the capital cities.

If you operate in the Territory, the audit will show you what engines currently say about your category. In our experience it is usually either nothing useful, or a business that no longer exists.

title: GEO for B2B SaaS: winning the comparison question
description: Software buyers now build their shortlist by asking an assistant. Why the comparison answer decides your pipeline, and how it gets decided.
body:
The B2B software buying journey used to start with a review site or a colleague's recommendation. Increasingly it starts with a question to an assistant: what are the best tools for this job, at our size, in our industry. The answer names three products, and everything downstream, the demos, the trials, the deal, flows from that shortlist.

If you are not in the three, you are not in the process, and you will never see the loss in any dashboard.

The comparison question is the whole game

SaaS buyers ask comparatively by nature. Which is better for us, how does X compare to Y, what should we use instead of Z. These questions do more to determine pipeline than any category level query, and they are decided by evidence you may not control.
